blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 3 (Chemical Bonding), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 State the Lewis concept of bonding. Explain the formation of the ionic bond in sodium chloride in its light. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chemical bond: the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions.

Lewis concept: atoms make bonds to complete their outermost shells and attain a noble gas-like configuration, mostly by forming an octet in the valence shell. It gives a simple explanation of the formation of all types of bonds.

Ionic bond: formed by the complete transfer of electrons from an atom with low ionization energy to an atom with high electron affinity.

Formation of NaCl:
• ₁₁Na (2, 8, 1) loses its outermost electron: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻. Na⁺ (2, 8) has the configuration of ₁₀Ne, the nearest noble gas.
• Cl (2, 8, 7) gains this electron: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) also has a noble gas arrangement.
• The oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held together by a strong ionic bond in the NaCl crystal (Fig. 3.1).

A similar bond is expected between group 1 and 2 metals and group 16 and 17 elements.

book_ref.quote: The oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held together by strong ionic bond in the crystal of NaCl.

blocks.prompt: 2 Define covalent and dative bonds. Explain the formation of dative bonds in the hydronium ion, carbon monoxide and ozone. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Covalent bond: formed by mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms; each atom completes its valence shell. It may be non-polar (Cl–Cl, H₂, F₂) or polar (H–Cl, H–Br, H₂O).

Dative (coordinate covalent) bond: formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms.

(i) Hydronium ion: H₂O has two covalent bonds and two lone pairs on O; the proton is electron-deficient. O donates a lone pair to H⁺:
H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (Fig. 3.3a)

(ii) Carbon monoxide: O shares two electrons with C to make a normal double covalent bond, but carbon's octet is still incomplete. O donates one of its lone pairs to C, making a dative bond (Fig. 3.3b).

(iii) Ozone: formed from an O₂ molecule and a free oxygen atom (O). One O atom of O₂ donates a lone pair to the free O atom, making a coordinate bond. The central O has three bonds (a double bond on one side and a coordinate bond on the other) and carries a positive charge; the accepting O carries a negative charge (Fig. 3.3c).

book_ref.quote: Let us consider the example of bond formation between H₂O and a proton (H⁺).

blocks.prompt: 3 What is an expanded octet? Explain the expanded octet of sulfur in the sulfate ion and the role of d orbitals in it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Polyatomic ions: ions made of two or more bonded atoms (they may be of one element, as in I₃⁻); their net charge is the formal charge. Except NH₄⁺, they mostly carry a negative charge: CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻.

Expanded octet: in some polyatomic ions the central atom violates the octet rule by expanding its electron density to higher orbitals. Examples: SO₄²⁻, ClO₄⁻, PO₄³⁻.

Sulfur in SO₄²⁻: in the Lewis structure S has two double bonds and two single bonds.
No. of valence electrons = 2 × (double bond electrons) + 2 × (single bond electrons) = 2(4) + 2(2) = 12
So S has 12 electrons and exceeds the octet by 4.

Role of d orbitals: the expansion is caused by the involvement of d orbitals, which accommodate the extra electrons. Ground-state S has two unpaired 3p electrons. Moving one 3p electron into 3d gives four unpaired electrons (3s² 3p³ 3d¹, used in SO₂); promoting one 3s electron as well gives six unpaired electrons (3s¹ 3p³ 3d²), the state needed for the six bonds of S in SO₄²⁻. This also explains the variable oxidation states of S.

book_ref.quote: In some polyatomic ions, the central atom violates the octet rule by expanding its electron density to the higher orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 4 Using the chapter's counting method (2 electrons for each single bond and each lone pair), find the number of electrons around the central atom in (i) PCl₅ (five P–Cl bonds) (ii) SF₆ (six S–F bonds) (iii) XeF₄ (four Xe–F bonds and two lone pairs), and state by how many electrons each exceeds the octet. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Count 2 electrons for every bond pair and every lone pair on the central atom, then subtract 8.

book_ref.quote: The number of valence electrons of the central atom can be calculated as follows,

steps: All three central atoms have expanded octets.
blocks.final_answer: P in PCl₅: 10 electrons (2 extra); S in SF₆: 12 (4 extra); Xe in XeF₄: 12 (4 extra).

blocks.prompt: 5 Electronegativities (given): H = 2.1, N = 3.0, O = 3.5, F = 4.0, Mg = 1.2, Li = 1.0. Using the chapter's limits, classify the bonds (i) O–H (ii) N–H (iii) Mg–O (iv) Li–F (v) F–F as pure covalent, polar covalent or ionic. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find each difference and compare: less than 0.4 pure covalent; 0.4 to 1.8 polar covalent; above 1.8 ionic.

book_ref.quote: The following figure graphically depicts the change in the nature of bond with electronegativity difference.

blocks.final_answer: O–H and N–H polar covalent; Mg–O and Li–F ionic; F–F pure covalent.

blocks.prompt: 6 What is a dipole moment? Explain how it helps to decide the shapes of molecules, taking examples of H₂O, SO₂, BeCl₂, BF₃ and CCl₄. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Dipole: a molecule with δ⁺ charge on one part and δ⁻ on the other; it has a dipole moment. In HF the bonded atoms are different, so electron distribution is uneven.
Dipole moment is a quantitative measurement of the polarity of a bond or molecule; unit Debye (D). It is directed from δ⁺ to δ⁻ (H → F in HF). Higher dipole moment means higher polarity.

Polyatomic molecules: the dipole moment depends on the structure.
• H₂O: dipole moment 1.85 D, from the H end towards O. A linear H–O–H would have zero dipole moment, so water is non-linear (v-shaped).
• SO₂: 1.61 D, in the opposite direction to that of water; it is angular.
• H₂S: non-linear; its polar bond moments do not cancel.

Zero dipole moment (symmetrical molecules):
• BeCl₂: linear, two equal Be–Cl moments at 180° in opposite directions cancel.
• BF₃: trigonal planar and symmetrical; zero dipole moment.
• CCl₄: four polar C–Cl bonds directed to the corners of a perfect tetrahedron; the moments cancel, so CCl₄ is non-polar.

Rule: molecules with the same ligands in a regular geometry have zero net dipole moment and are non-polar.

book_ref.quote: For compounds having more than two atoms, the dipole moment depends on the structure of the molecule.

blocks.prompt: 7 State the basic idea and postulates of the VSEPR model. Give the steps used to determine the shape of a molecule, taking CCl₄ as an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The VSEPR model (Sidgwick and Powell, 1940) describes the shapes of molecules from the electron pairs around the central atom. A molecule takes a shape in which repulsions among the valence electron pairs are minimum; the pairs stay as far apart as possible, and this arrangement decides the geometry.

Postulates:
1. Both lone pairs and bond pairs take part in deciding the geometry.
2. Electron pairs stay at maximum distance apart to avoid repulsions.
3. Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs and compress them. Repulsion order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp.
4. The two pairs of a double bond and three pairs of a triple bond have higher charge density but are regarded as single pairs.
5. Highly electronegative atoms on the central atom decrease bond pair repulsions but give stronger lone pair repulsion.

Steps (CCl₄):
1. Choose the central atom: the least electronegative atom or the element with the fewest atoms (C).
2. Count all electron pairs around it: C has 4 bond pairs and no lone pair.
3. Total pairs give the electron pair geometry: 4 pairs, tetrahedral.
4. Find the actual shape excluding lone pairs: CCl₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°).

book_ref.quote: In order to have the minimal repulsions, the electron pairs arrange themselves at farthest possible distances.

blocks.prompt: 8 Using the VSEPR model, explain the shapes of BeCl₂, BF₃, SnCl₂ and SO₃. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
AB₂ (linear): in BeCl₂ the central Be has two bond pairs and no lone pair. The two pairs arrange at 180° to minimize repulsion, so BeCl₂ is linear (Fig. 3.9).

AB₃ (trigonal planar): three electron pairs arrange at 120° at maximum distance. BF₃ has three bond pairs; it is trigonal planar with each F–B–F angle 120° (Fig. 3.10). Group 3 hydrides AlH₃, GaH₃, BH₃ are similar.

AB₃ with a lone pair: Sn in SnCl₂ has 4 outer electrons; it forms two bonds with Cl and keeps two electrons as a lone pair. The lone pair occupies one corner of the triangle (distorted trigonal geometry in the vapour phase), so SnCl₂ is v-shaped with angle less than 120° (Fig. 3.11).

AB₃ with multiple bonds: in SO₃ all three regions are S=O bonds (each counted as one pair), so SO₃ is perfectly trigonal with 120° angles (Fig. 3.12).

book_ref.quote: In AB₃ type molecules, the central atom is surrounded by three electron pairs

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain, with the VSEPR model, why the bond angles decrease in the order CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°). Why is the angle of NF₃ even smaller (102.5°)? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All four are AB₄ systems: four electron pairs around the central atom give a tetrahedral electron pair geometry.

• CH₄: four bond pairs, no lone pair. The pairs point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron; each H–C–H angle is 109.5°. SiH₄, GeH₄, CCl₄ are similar.
• NH₃: three bond pairs and one lone pair. The lone pair occupies more space and repels the bond pairs more strongly (lp-bp > bp-bp), so the angle falls to 107°; the shape is triangular pyramidal.
• H₂O: two bond pairs and two lone pairs. The lp-lp repulsion is strongest, so the angle falls further to 104.5°; the shape is angular (v-shaped).

So the more lone pairs, the greater the compression of the bond angle.

NF₃ (102.5°): (i) the strongly polar N–F bonds make N pull the lone pair closer to its nucleus, so it repels the bonding electrons more strongly; (ii) the N–F bond pairs lie closer to F than to N; the increased distance weakens their mutual repulsion and lets the bonds come closer.

book_ref.quote: In this type of molecules, the charge clouds due to four electron pairs avoid their electrostatic repulsions

header: Bond pairs / lone pairs; shape; angle

blocks.prompt: 10 Explain, with the VSEPR model, how lone pairs change the shapes of AB₅ and AB₆ systems, taking the tri-iodide ion and XeF₄ as examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
AB₅ (trigonal bipyramid): five pairs are evenly distributed at the corners of a trigonal bipyramid: three in a planar triangle and two on an axis perpendicular to it. With no lone pair (PCl₅) the angles are 120° in the plane and 90° between axial and planar atoms.

Tri-iodide ion [I₃]⁻: the central I has five electron pairs, two bond pairs and three lone pairs, so the electron pair geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. The lone pairs occupy the corners of the trigonal region and the two I atoms sit on the apices, one above and one below the plane. Excluding the lone pairs, I₃⁻ is linear, the I atoms being 180° apart (Fig. 3.18). The change here is more dramatic than in AB₃ and AB₄.

AB₆ (octahedral): six pairs: four at the corners of a planar square and two on a perpendicular axis; all angles 90°, e.g. SF₆.

XeF₄: four bond pairs and two lone pairs. The two lone pairs stay farthest apart, at 180° (on the axis). Excluding them, XeF₄ is square planar with all F–Xe–F angles 90° (Fig. 3.20).

book_ref.quote: Just as in the AB₃ and AB₄ types, the presence of lone pairs in AB₅ system also changes the shape

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the application of the VSEPR model in drug designing, with the example of aspirin. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Drugs: chemical substances that prevent, diagnose or treat a disease. They act at specific points or processes in the body called targets or substrates (receptors such as enzymes, proteins, nucleic acids and cellular pathways), through their bioactive molecules called ligands. A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand by binding. Each drug interacts with a specific target to a different degree: specificity.

Role of shape: molecular shape decides how a drug interacts with its target. Only ligands of suitable shape fit the active site, as a specific key fits a specific lock (drug A binds; drug B, of the wrong shape, cannot). The VSEPR model is used to find shapes in biological systems: substrate recognition, ligand specificity or selectivity, and antibody recognition.

Aspirin: an analgesic (painkiller). It interacts with the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) by binding to its active site through the acetyl group (–OCCH₃). The shapes of the COX active site and the acetyl group are compatible, so binding succeeds and blocks COX, which is a cause of pain (Fig. 3.21).

book_ref.quote: VSEPR model is successfully applied in determining the shapes of various biological systems

blocks.prompt: 12 State the postulates of valence bond theory. Describe the types of overlap that form sigma bonds, with one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
VSEPR explains shapes but not why bonds form; VBT explains both, treating a molecule as a combination of atoms.

Postulates:
1. A covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms with similar energy overlap.
2. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond.
3. Covalent bonds are directional; the direction depends on the shape and mode of the overlapping orbitals.

Sigma (σ) bond: formed by linear (head-on) overlap of two half-filled orbitals on adjacent atoms along the nuclear axis. Both s and p orbitals can form it.
• s-s overlap: H₂. Each H has a half-filled s orbital; after overlap the electrons pair up and the electron density is symmetrical around the two nuclei (Fig. 3.22).
• s-p overlap: HCl. The half-filled s orbital of H overlaps the half-filled p orbital of Cl; the electron density is higher near Cl (more electronegative), so HCl is polar (Fig. 3.23).
• p-p overlap: Cl₂. p orbitals of two Cl atoms overlap on the nuclear axis; the density is symmetrical as both have the same electronegativity (Fig. 3.24).

book_ref.quote: The postulates of VBT are given below

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain the formation of the double bond in the oxygen molecule according to VBT. How is the bent H₂S molecule formed, and why is its angle smaller than that of water? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Double bond in O₂ (O=O): each O atom has two unpaired electrons in perpendicular p orbitals (px and py).
• The px orbitals of the two atoms overlap end-to-end linearly, giving a σ bond.
• The py orbitals are parallel to each other; they overlap sideways, two lobes above and two below the plane of the nuclei, giving a π bond (Fig. 3.26).
So the O atoms are doubly bonded through one σ and one π bond.

H₂S: S has two half-filled 3p orbitals (3py and 3pz). Each overlaps the 1s orbital of one H atom, giving two σ bonds. The molecule is non-linear (v-shaped) with a bond angle of 92° (Fig. 3.25).

Comparison: the H–O–H angle is 104.5° but H–S–H is 92°, because the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion.

book_ref.quote: The px orbitals on the two oxygen atoms are oriented in such a way that they overlap end-to-end linearly.

blocks.prompt: 14 Define hybridization and give its main features. Explain sp³ hybridization taking methane as an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hybridization: a process in which atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes mix to form a new set of equivalent orbitals of the same energy and shape.

Features:
• It is mixing of orbitals in a single atom (or ion).
• Only orbitals of comparable (close) energies mix.
• The number of mixing orbitals equals the number of hybrid orbitals formed.

sp³ hybridization: one s orbital (low energy, spherical) and three p orbitals (higher energy, dumbbell shaped) intermix to give four sp³ hybrid orbitals of the same energy and shape, arranged tetrahedrally.
Carbon: ground state ₆C 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹; excited state 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹; these four orbitals mix to give four half-filled sp³ orbitals (Fig. 3.27). Each sp³ orbital has two lobes, one larger and one smaller.

Methane: the four sp³ orbitals of C overlap separately with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms, forming four sp³-s σ bonds directed to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, H–C–H = 109.5°.

book_ref.quote: Hybridization is a process of mixing of orbitals in a single atom (or ion).

blocks.prompt: 15 Explain sp² hybridization in BF₃ and sp hybridization in BeCl₂. Compare sp, sp² and sp³ hybridization. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
sp² (BF₃): ₅B ground state 2s² 2px¹; excited 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹. One s and two p orbitals mix to give three half-filled sp² orbitals in a trigonal plane at 120°. Each overlaps a half-filled 2pz orbital of F, so BF₃ is triangular planar with F–B–F = 120° (Fig. 3.30).

sp (BeCl₂): ₄Be ground state 2s²; excited 2s¹ 2px¹. One s and one p orbital mix to give two sp orbitals of the same energy and shape, linear at 180°. Each overlaps a half-filled p orbital of Cl, so BeCl₂ is linear (Fig. 3.32).

book_ref.quote: In sp hybridization, one s (low energy and spherical) and one p orbital

blocks.prompt: 16 State the postulates of molecular orbital theory. Describe the formation of molecular orbitals by s-s overlap in H₂ and by head-on and sideways approach of p orbitals. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Postulates:
1. Atomic orbitals of the combining atoms overlap to form new molecular orbitals, characteristic of the whole molecule.
2. Orbitals overlap through lobes of suitable sign of the wave function (one lobe of a p orbital is '+', the other '−').
3. Two atomic orbitals form two molecular orbitals: same-sign overlap gives a bonding MO (σ or π) of lower energy; opposite-sign overlap gives an anti-bonding MO (σ* or π*) of higher energy than the parent orbitals.
4. Bond order = (a − b)/2, where a = bonding and b = anti-bonding electrons.

s-s overlap (H₂): two 1s orbitals give two MOs. The bonding MO is symmetrical about the nuclear axis; the anti-bonding MO has its electron density away from the nuclei (Fig. 3.34).

Head-on approach: p orbitals approach along the same axis (x-axis), giving σ(2px) bonding and σ*(2px) anti-bonding MOs.

Sideways approach: py or pz orbitals with parallel axes interact to form π MOs. Bonding π(2py), π(2pz) have zero electron density on the nuclear axis (nodal plane); anti-bonding π*(2py), π*(2pz) have the least electron density in the inter-nuclear region (Fig. 3.35).

book_ref.quote: The atomic orbitals overlap with the lobe having suitable sign of the wave function of the orbital.

blocks.prompt: 17 With the help of molecular orbital theory, explain why He₂ does not exist while N₂ has a triple bond. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
He₂: He is 1s². The 1s orbitals of two He atoms combine to give bonding σ1s and anti-bonding σ*1s MOs (Fig. 3.36). Of the four electrons, two enter σ1s and two enter σ*1s.
Bond order of He₂ = (2 − 2)/2 = 0
Zero bond order means no bond, so He₂ is not formed.

N₂: ₇N is 1s², 2s², 2px¹, 2py¹, 2pz¹. The 2s orbitals give σ2s and σ*2s; the 2p orbitals give six MOs. Increasing order of energy:
σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px
The six 2p electrons fill π2py, π2pz and σ2px; no 2p anti-bonding orbital is occupied (Fig. 3.37).
Bond order of N₂ = (6 − 0)/2 = 3
So the N atoms are joined by three bonds, one σ and two π: a triple bond.

book_ref.quote: For a successful formation of He₂ molecule, 1s orbitals of two He atoms must combine

blocks.prompt: 18 Describe the molecular orbital picture of the oxygen molecule. How does MOT explain its bond order and its paramagnetic nature? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
MO energy order for O₂ (Fig. 3.38):
σ2s < σ*2s < σ2px < π2py = π2pz < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px

Filling the 2p electrons: six enter the bonding σ2px, π2py and π2pz, and two enter the anti-bonding π* orbitals, one in π*(2py) and one in π*(2pz) (unpaired).

Bond order = (6 − 2)/2 = 2, so the O atoms are joined by one σ and one π bond: a double bond (O=O).

Paramagnetism: paramagnetic substances are attracted by a magnetic field and have one or more unpaired electrons; many unpaired electrons make a substance strongly paramagnetic. The two unpaired electrons in π*(2py) and π*(2pz) give O₂ a net magnetic field that interacts with an external field. So O₂ is paramagnetic: liquid oxygen is attracted and gets suspended between the poles of a strong magnet. MOT successfully explains this behaviour.

blocks.prompt: 19 Using bond order = (a − b)/2, find the bond order of diatomic species having (i) 8 bonding and 2 anti-bonding electrons (ii) 8 bonding and 4 anti-bonding electrons (iii) 6 bonding and 4 anti-bonding electrons (iv) 4 bonding and 4 anti-bonding electrons. Arrange them in order of decreasing bond order and say which cannot exist. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put a and b in the formula for each; a bond order of zero means no bond.

book_ref.quote: and is taken as half of the difference between the number of bonding electrons (say a) and anti-bonding electrons (say b)

steps: Order: (i) 3 > (ii) 2 > (iii) 1 > (iv) 0; species (iv) cannot exist, like He₂.
blocks.final_answer: Bond orders 3, 2, 1 and 0; the species with bond order 0 cannot exist.

blocks.prompt: 20 What are intermolecular forces? Name their types and explain how they differ from chemical bonds in nature and strength. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Intermolecular (van der Waals) forces: binding forces like chemical bonds, but the attraction between molecules is much weaker. They exist between all kinds of atoms and molecules when sufficiently close, bring molecules together and give particular physical properties in the gaseous, liquid and solid states.

Types:
1. Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces.
2. Permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.
3. Hydrogen bonding.

Difference from chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are true chemical bonds; they form new species through transfer and sharing of electrons and affect chemical properties. Intermolecular forces bring molecules closer and influence physical properties. Being weak, van der Waals forces are usually not termed pure chemical bonds. The distinctive feature is strength, measured by bond energy (Table 3.4).

book_ref.quote: Intermolecular forces are also considered as binding forces just like chemical bonds.

rows: Form new species by transfer and sharing of electrons.
Weak: hydrogen bonding 20-50, dipole-dipole 5-20, van der Waals 1-20 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 21 Define bond energy. Explain the factors on which it depends, using the data for H–X bonds and carbon-carbon bonds. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bond energy: the average amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of a substance. It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction; unit kJ mol⁻¹. It measures the strength of a bond and its reactivity.

Factors: (1) electronegativity difference of the bonded atoms; (2) size of the atoms.

Electronegativity difference: for H–X (X = F, Cl, Br, I) the bond energy rises with increasing electronegativity difference. Greater difference gives greater bond polarity, which adds an attractive force binding the atoms. So H–F (565) > H–Cl (427) > H–Br (363) > H–I (295) kJ mol⁻¹.

Multiple bonds: energies of multiple bonds are greater than those of single bonds: C≡C (839) > C=C (614) > C–C (347) kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: The strength of a bond depends upon the following factors.

blocks.prompt: 22 Using average bond energies from Table 3.2 (C–H 413, H–H 432, N≡N 941, O–H 467 kJ mol⁻¹), calculate the energy needed to break (i) all C–H bonds in 2 mol of CH₄ (ii) all bonds in 2 mol of H₂ (iii) all bonds in 0.5 mol of N₂ (iv) all O–H bonds in 1 mol of H₂O. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Energy = (moles of bonds) × (bond energy); moles of bonds = moles of substance × number of such bonds per molecule.

book_ref.quote: Let us consider the role played by electronegativity difference.

steps: (i) CH₄ has 4 C–H bonds: 2 × 4 = 8 mol bonds; 8 × 413 = 3304 kJ.
(ii) H₂ has 1 H–H bond: 2 mol bonds; 2 × 432 = 864 kJ.
(iii) N₂ has 1 N≡N bond: 0.5 mol bonds; 0.5 × 941 = 470.5 kJ.
(iv) H₂O has 2 O–H bonds: 2 mol bonds; 2 × 467 = 934 kJ.

blocks.prompt: 23 Covalent radii (given): C = 77 pm, F = 64 pm, Si = 117 pm. (i) Calculate the expected C–F and Si–F bond lengths. (ii) Using the observed values C–F = 135 pm (Table 3.3) and Si–F = 155 pm (in SiF₄), find the shortening in each and its percentage. (iii) Explain the shortening. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Expected bond length = sum of covalent radii; shortening = expected − observed; percentage = shortening/expected × 100.

book_ref.quote: The electronegativity difference causes an ionic character in the covalent bond.

steps: (i) C–F expected = 77 + 64 = 141 pm; Si–F expected = 117 + 64 = 181 pm.

(iii) The electronegativity difference gives the covalent bond ionic character; the additional attraction between the bonded atoms shortens the bond. The larger shortening for Si–F shows its greater ionic character.
blocks.final_answer: Expected C–F 141 pm, Si–F 181 pm; shortening 6 pm (4.3%) and 26 pm (14.4%), due to ionic character.

blocks.prompt: 24 Define bond length. How is it determined? Explain the effect of atomic size, electronegativity difference and the nature of the bond on bond length, with examples from Table 3.3. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bond length: the distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond. It is determined experimentally by physical techniques such as electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction or spectral studies. It is governed by electronegativity, size and the nature of the bond (single, double or triple).

Size of atoms: bond length increases with atomic size. C–F 135 pm < C–Cl 180 pm < C–Br 196 pm < C–I 214 pm; the Cl atom is much larger than F.

Electronegativity difference: a larger difference shortens the bond. The Si–F bond in SiF₄ is near 155 pm, while the covalent radii (Si = 117 pm, F = 64 pm) give 181 pm. The electronegativity difference causes ionic character, and the extra attraction shortens the bond.

Nature of the bond: C–C 154 pm > C=C 133 pm > C≡C 120 pm; multiple bonds are shorter.

book_ref.quote: With an increase in size of the atoms, the covalent bond length also increases.

blocks.prompt: 25 Compare ionic, covalent and metallic bonds and intermolecular forces in terms of their bond energies. Why is the metallic bond weaker than ionic and covalent bonds? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are true chemical bonds; they form new species by transfer and sharing of electrons and affect chemical properties, while intermolecular forces bring molecules closer and affect physical properties. The distinctive feature is strength, measured by bond energy.

From Table 3.4: ionic bond in NaCl (760 kJ mol⁻¹) is the strongest, followed by the covalent O–H bond in water (464), hydrogen bonding (20-50), permanent dipole-dipole forces (5-20) and van der Waals forces (1-20). So the ionic bond is the strongest form of bonding, and chemical bonds are generally much stronger than intermolecular forces.

Metallic bond: mostly described in terms of electrostatic forces, though some theories suggest covalent nature. Its average bond energy is 100-150 kJ mol⁻¹, weaker than both ionic and covalent bonds. A satisfactory argument for its low strength is the extensive delocalization of electrons within the metallic crystal.

book_ref.quote: The metallic bond is mostly elaborated in terms of electrostatic forces
